procedural_history.originating_court: Complaint was registered with the police.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The appellants unsuccessfully sought the intervention of the High Court of Patna under Art. 226 of the Constitution in Cr. W.J.C. No. 11 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a petition (Cr. W.J.C. No. 11 of 1966) in the High Court of Patna under Article 226 of the Constitution, seeking to stop the investigation against them. The High Court dismissed their petition on July 4, 1966.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave from the judgment and order of the Patna High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the complaint made before the police disclosed a cognizable offence empowering the police to investigate.

facts: A complaint was registered against the appellants, office bearers of a sugar company, for failing to pay for sugarcane within the prescribed time.
The offence complained of was punishable with three years' imprisonment.
law: Under the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), an offence is defined as 'cognizable' in Section 4(1)(f).
The 2nd Schedule of the Cr.P.C. classifies offences, and those punishable with three years' imprisonment fall under this schedule as cognizable.
application: The Court examined the potential punishment for the offence alleged in the complaint, which was three years' imprisonment.
It determined that because the punishment was three years, the offence falls within the 2nd Schedule of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Consequently, the offence met the definition of a 'cognizable offence' as defined in Section 4(1)(f) of the Code.
As the offence was cognizable, the police were legally empowered to investigate the complaint.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, finding that the complaint did disclose a cognizable offence. The Court reasoned that since the alleged offence was punishable with three years' imprisonment, it was classified as a cognizable offence under the Code of Criminal Procedure, thereby giving the police the authority to investigate.

issue.issue_text: Whether Parliament was competent to enact a law relating to the control of sugarcane, which was contended to be within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State.

facts: The appellants argued that Parliament lacked the competence to pass a law controlling sugarcane.
Their contention was that sugarcane is a part of 'agriculture', a subject falling under the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State.
law: The Court identified Entry 33 of List III (the Concurrent List) of the Constitution as the source of Parliament's legislative power.
Entry 33 empowers Parliament to legislate on the 'production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs'.
The Essential Commodities Act defines 'essential commodity' to include 'foodstuffs' (Section 2(a)(v)).
The Act further clarifies that 'food-crops include sugarcane' (Section 2(b)).
application: The Court reasoned that since Entry 33 of List III gives Parliament concurrent power to legislate on foodstuffs, and the Essential Commodities Act explicitly includes sugarcane within the definition of food-crops/foodstuffs, Parliament was acting within its constitutional authority.
The Court noted that Parliament had made the necessary declaration that it was in the public interest to control foodstuffs, thus validly invoking its power under Entry 33.
Therefore, the provisions of the Act, which allow the Central Government to control the production, supply, distribution, and price of essential commodities, could be validly applied to sugarcane.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the contention and held that Parliament was competent to enact the law controlling sugarcane. The power was derived from Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution, which allows Parliament to legislate on foodstuffs, and the Act specifically includes sugarcane within this category.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned order resulted in a violation of the fundamental right under Art. 19(1) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellants, office bearers of a sugar company, were being investigated for failing to pay sellers for sugarcane within the time prescribed by the Sugarcane (Control) Order.
They argued that this order, which mandated timely payment, violated their fundamental right under Article 19(1) of the Constitution.
law: The Supreme Court considered the scope of the fundamental rights guaranteed to citizens under Article 19(1) of the Constitution.
application: The Court analyzed the nature of the right being claimed by the appellants.
It determined that the appellants were essentially asserting a right not to pay for goods they had purchased, or at least a right to pay for them whenever they pleased.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' contention, stating that there is no fundamental right conferred on a buyer to not pay the price of goods purchased or to pay for them at their own convenience. Therefore, the order mandating timely payment did not contravene Article 19(1).

issue.issue_text: Whether cognizance of the offence could have been taken in view of s. 11 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.

facts: The case was at the stage of a police investigation following a complaint.
The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the investigation itself.
law: Section 11 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, governs how a court can take cognizance of an offence under the Act.
application: The Supreme Court observed that the proceedings were still at the investigation stage.
No court had yet been asked to take, or had taken, cognizance of the alleged offence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the argument based on Section 11 was premature. Since no court had yet taken cognizance of the case, the question of whether such cognizance was proper under the Act did not arise at that stage.

issue.issue_text: Whether the investigation being carried on against the appellants was in accordance with law.

facts: The appellants are office bearers of a sugar company.
A police complaint was registered against them for failing to pay for sugarcane within the prescribed time, an offense under the Sugarcane (Control) Order and the Essential Commodities Act.
The police began an investigation into this complaint.
The appellants challenged the legality of this investigation, arguing that the police were not empowered to investigate it.
law: An offense punishable with three years' imprisonment is classified as a 'cognizable offence' under the 2nd Schedule and Section 4(1)(f) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P.C.).
Police are legally empowered to investigate cognizable offenses.
The issue of a court taking 'cognizance' of a case is a separate stage that occurs after the investigation is complete and is not relevant to the police's authority to investigate.
application: The Court first examined the appellants' claim that the complaint did not disclose a cognizable offense, which would mean the police had no power to investigate.
The Court noted that the offense in question was punishable with three years' imprisonment.
Applying the Criminal Procedure Code, the Court determined that this punishment makes the offense cognizable.
Because the offense was cognizable, the Court concluded that the police were lawfully permitted to investigate the complaint.
The Court also considered the appellants' argument related to Section 11 of the Essential Commodities Act, which concerns how a court takes cognizance of an offense.
It found this argument to be 'premature' because the case was still at the investigation stage, and no court had yet taken cognizance of the matter.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' challenge, holding that the investigation was in accordance with the law. It found that the offense was cognizable, which legally empowered the police to investigate, and dismissed the other arguments as premature.

cases.case_name: Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors.
cases.principle: Parliament has the competence to legislate in respect of the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution, Parliament is competent to enact legislation to regulate the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs, which includes food crops. A rule created under such legislation that mandates timely payment for purchased goods does not violate the fundamental right under Article 19(1), as there is no fundamental right for a buyer to not pay the price of goods purchased. Such central legislation, enacted by a competent authority, can alter or amend pre-constitutional state laws on the same subject.
obiter: The question of whether cognizance of an offence could be taken under a specific section of an Act is premature if no court has yet taken cognizance of the alleged offence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the investigation against the appellants for failing to pay for sugarcane was validly initiated. The challenges to the investigation were rejected because Parliament was constitutionally competent to legislate on sugarcane as a foodstuff, the resulting order did not violate any fundamental rights, and the procedural objection regarding cognizance of the offence was premature as that stage had not yet been reached.
legal_tests_applied: Constitutional Interpretation (Distribution of Legislative Powers): The court examined Parliament's legislative competence by referencing Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution to determine if it could regulate 'foodstuffs' like sugarcane.

Ripeness Doctrine: The court applied the principle that a legal question is not ready for judicial decision until a controversy is concrete and immediate. It found the issue of 'cognizance' was not ripe because no court had yet taken cognizance of the offence.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Parliament lacked competence to legislate on sugarcane failed because the court found that under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution, Parliament is empowered to legislate on the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs, which includes sugarcane.
The claim that the impugned order violated Article 19(1) was rejected on the grounds that there is no fundamental right conferred on a buyer to not pay the price of goods they have purchased.

The contention that cognizance of the offence could not be taken under Section 11 of the Act was dismissed as premature, because the case was still at the investigation stage and no court had yet taken cognizance.
The argument that the power to enforce payment was merely implied was incorrect; the court found that Sub-rule (3) of rule 3 specifically provides for this power.
why_respondent_won: Parliament's competence to enact the Essential Commodities Act was affirmed based on its constitutional power over foodstuffs under Entry 33 of List III, which had been declared by law to be expedient in the public interest.
The court accepted the respondent's position that the challenge regarding cognizance of the offence was premature, as the matter was still under investigation.
The investigation was found to be valid as it was based on an alleged violation of an explicit provision (Sub-rule (3) of rule 3) made under a constitutionally valid Act.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the legislative policy determination that it is 'expedient in public interest' for the central government to exercise control over foodstuffs, thereby justifying Parliament's enactment of the controlling law.
